newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends mixed, Canadian dollar roars.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends mixed, Canadian dollar roars.

text.p: The dollar fell against the Canadian dollar Thursday after the Bank of Canada surprised investors by raising official interest rates.
The dollar rose slightly against the German mark after a Bundesbank official suggested official German interest rates might fall, and ended mixed against other currencies.
The small rise in Canadian rates triggered heavy selling of U.S. dollars for Canadian paper, currency traders said.
"We saw a frenzy of Canadian buying on that news. That took everyone by surprise," said Seth Garrett, chief dealer at Credit Suiss First Boston.
The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3817 from C$1.3937 Wednesday afternoon.

The U.S. currency edged higher to 1.7260 marks from 1.7240 Wednesday, but fell to 113.10 Japanese yen from 113.92. The British pound rose to $1.6650 from $1.6635. The dollar fell to 1.4365 Swiss francs from 1.4370.
The dollar ended at 5.8240 French francs, up from 5.8175.

Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen triggered dollar buying in European trading when he told an audience in Frankfurt he could not rule out a cut in interest rates, even though he did not see one on the horizon.
Lower German rates would boost the relative value of dollar-based investments and the prospect fuelled minor dollar buying, traders said.
"You couldn't really say the dollar was strong, but nobody was wild about buying German marks," said Bruce Giammattei, senior trader at Mellon Bank.
Investors also bought the yen on the talk of lower German rates, and the dollar fell slightly against the yen as a result.
"The dollar got sold down pretty convincingly against the yen," Giammattei said.

The dollar also rose against the French franc after news that French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin instructed his ministers to focus on job creation and not on reducing the federal budget deficit in the year ahead.
Investors have serious questions about France's ability to meet the deficit target to qualify for proposed European monetary union in 1999, and the French franc was sold on the news.
"The only reason I can think of to own the French franc is that it might be part of EMU. Should EMU fail, the French franc would suffer a great deal," Giammattei said.
